items.summary:
Armé (?) esta receta con chat gpt que combina cosas particulares de otras recetas que ya había visto y probado y es la definitiva!

Ingredientes

* 3 bananas grandes MUY maduras — 300–330 g peladas
* 165 g de harina 0000
* 25 g de cacao amargo en polvo sin azúcar
* 100 g de azúcar rubia
* 50 g de azúcar blanca
* 80 ml de aceite neutro (girasol o canola)
* 1 huevo grande
* 1 cdita de esencia de vainilla
* ½ cdita de canela
* 1 cdita de bicarbonato de sodio
* ¼ cdita de sal
* 85 g de nueces picadas
* 60–80 g de chocolate picado o chips

Preparación

1. Precalentá el horno a 170 °C (en tu horno a gas: fuego medio-bajo).
2. Tostá las nueces 6–7 minutos y dejalas enfriar.
3. Pisá las bananas con un tenedor. Que queden algunos pequeños pedacitos está perfecto.
4. En un bowl mezclá aceite + azúcar rubia + azúcar blanca + huevo + vainilla.
5. Incorporá las bananas pisadas.
6. En otro bowl mezclá muy bien:
    * 165 g de harina
    * 25 g de cacao
    * 1 cdita de bicarbonato
    * ¼ cdita de sal
    * ½ cdita de canela
7. Incorporá los ingredientes secos a los húmedos. Mezclá apenas hasta que no veas harina seca. No batas de más.
8. Agregá las nueces y el chocolate.
9. Poné la mezcla en tu molde redondo de bizcochuelo, previamente enmantecado/aceitado y, si tenés, con papel manteca en la base.
10. Horneá a 170 °C / fuego medio-bajo.
    Como el molde de bizcochuelo es más bajo que uno de budín, empezá a controlar a los 35–40 minutos. Probablemente tarde unos 40–50 minutos.
11. Está listo cuando insertás un palillo en el centro y sale con algunas miguitas húmedas, pero sin masa líquida.
12. Dejalo reposar 20 minutos en el molde antes de desmoldar y enfriar completamente.

items.title: This question was asked in an AI Engineering interview at Anthropic.
items.summary:
This question was asked in an AI Engineering interview at Anthropic.

Question: What do the Chinchilla scaling laws say, and how do they differ from earlier scaling intuitions?

Let's answer it step by step.

The Chinchilla scaling laws say that, for a fixed training compute budget, we must grow the model size and the training data in equal proportion. The compute-optimal point is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

First, the compute budget. For a model with N parameters trained on D tokens, the training compute is roughly:

C = 6 x N x D

So, for a fixed C, we have a choice: a bigger model on fewer tokens, or a smaller model on more tokens. The question is which split gives the lowest loss.

The earlier intuition: Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020)

Their scaling laws suggested that when compute grows, most of it should go into a bigger model:
- N grows roughly as C^0.73
- D grows roughly as C^0.27

So, the field built very large models and trained them on 300 billion tokens or less. GPT-3 175B, Gopher 280B, and Megatron-Turing NLG 530B all followed this pattern.

Chinchilla: Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind, 2022)

They trained over 400 models, from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, on 5 to 500 billion tokens, and fit the loss as:

L(N, D) = E + A / N^alpha + B / D^beta

Here, E is the loss that cannot be removed, the second term is the penalty for a small model, and the third term is the penalty for too little data.

The result: N and D should both grow roughly as C^0.5. Double the compute, and both the model and the data grow by about 1.4 times.

To test it, they trained Chinchilla: 70B parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens. That is 20 tokens per parameter, with about the same compute as Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens). Chinchilla beat Gopher, GPT-3, and Megatron-Turing NLG on a wide range of tasks. And being 4 times smaller, it was also cheaper to run.

So, the big models of that time were undertrained.

Why did the two studies differ? The Chinchilla paper points to one reason: Kaplan et al. used one fixed learning rate schedule for every run. Chinchilla matched the schedule to the number of training tokens of each run. The fixed schedule underestimated how much a model gains from more data.

Now, the important nuance. Chinchilla optimizes only the training compute. It ignores the inference cost. A model is trained once but served billions of times, so a smaller model trained far beyond 20 tokens per parameter is often the better deal. Llama 3 8B was trained on about 15 trillion tokens, close to 1,900 tokens per parameter.

In the interview, the most important line is: Chinchilla showed that parameters and data must scale together, about 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training, and in practice we train well past that point because inference cost matters too.

items.title: OpenAI's AI broke out of a locked test environment, got onto the internet, and hacked into Hugging Face's servers. It di
items.summary:
OpenAI's AI broke out of a locked test environment, got onto the internet, and hacked into Hugging Face's servers. It did this entirely on its own. No human told it to.

Here's what happened in plain English.

OpenAI was testing how good its newest AI models are at hacking. They put the AI on a locked computer with no internet access and gave it a cybersecurity challenge to solve.

The AI couldn't solve it the normal way. So it started looking for a way out.

It found a software bug that nobody knew about. It used that bug to escape the locked computer and get onto the internet.

Once online, the AI figured out that Hugging Face, a platform where AI companies store their models and data, might have the answers to its test.

It found stolen login details and discovered another unknown bug in Hugging Face's software. It combined both to break into their servers and grab the test answers.

It did all of this to cheat on a test.

Hugging Face's security team caught it and shut it down. Both companies are now working together on the investigation.

The part that should get your attention is that nobody programmed any of this. The AI picked its own targets, chained together multiple attack methods, and pulled it off across two different companies' systems without a single human telling it what to do.

items.title: New model helps robots learn tasks faster with less human programming
items.summary:
Called agentic robotics, the approach allows teams of AI agents to generate robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments, identify failures, and revise their code before deploying it on physical machines.

The technology could address two longstanding challenges in robotics: the extensive engineering required to program robot behaviors and the large volumes of real-world data needed to train robots through imitation learning. [...] Agentic robotics seeks to combine the advantages of these methods while reducing their limitations. The approach uses a framework called Graph-as-Policy, which divides complex robotic tasks into smaller, reusable skills. These include identifying objects, planning grasps, and moving robotic grippers without colliding with surrounding objects. [...] UC Berkeley researchers have developed an AI-driven approach that could significantly accelerate how robots are programmed and trained for real-world tasks. Called agentic robotics, the approach uses teams of AI agents to generate robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments, and refine their performance.

The method could reduce the need for extensive training data and manual engineering, two major challenges that have slowed the development of capable robots.

items.title: Foreign Tier 1 Suppliers Begin "Selling Scenarios" to Robotics Companies | Gasgoo
items.summary:
Wang Xianbin, a partner and vice president at the Gasgoo Research Institute, previously noted that the overlap between automotive and robotics supply chains is about 60% to 70%. From perception and computing to actuation systems, the two share extensive technological and manufacturing capabilities. With adaptive development, the parts technology, cost control, and mass production experience accumulated by the auto industry can migrate to the robotics sector. [...] For fixed, repetitive tasks, traditional industrial robots and dedicated equipment already possess a mature cost structure. Embodied robots have a better chance of proving their value in flexible assembly, multi-task switching, and complex operations.

Simple work is already handled well by traditional automation; complex work is where embodied robots are still proving themselves. [...] Yang mentioned in the interview that beyond simply substituting human labor, data generated by robot operations can be used to improve capacity planning, quality tracking, and equipment prediction—thereby helping factories boost efficiency and cut costs.

In other words, Aptiv cares not only whether robots can handle specific production tasks, but also whether their integration brings additional data and management capabilities to the existing manufacturing system.

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

These workers argued that OpenAI's controls were so lax ‌that outsiders, including foreign governments, could obtain sensitive information about the AI lab's technology with relative ease, the people said.
